output.chapter_summary: Book basis: The body has four main tissue types: epithelial tissue provides covering or lining, muscular tissue helps movement, neural tissue responds to stimuli, and connective tissue supports, links and cushions. The supplied material compares epithelial types by location, structure and function; distinguishes skeletal, cardiac and visceral muscle; identifies blood cells, compact bone, hyaline cartilage, areolar tissue and adipose tissue; and follows messages through successive neurons. Outside explanations are separately labelled and limited to foundations and mechanisms needed to understand these book examples.

concepts.name: Four major body tissues and their functional identities
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: The body has mainly four types of tissue: epithelial, muscular, neural and connective. Their identifying functions are, respectively, covering or lining; helping movement; responding to stimuli; and supporting, linking and cushioning. Use these functions as the first classification step before examining the cells and arrangements within each group.

concepts.name: Epithelial sheets, barriers and the basement membrane
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Epithelium covers most organs and cavities and forms a barrier that keeps different body systems separate. Its tightly packed cells form a continuous sheet, with little cementing material and almost no intercellular spaces; it is usually separated from underlying tissue by an extracellular fibrous basement membrane. Outside explanation: The close packing helps explain the barrier function, and the basement membrane beneath the sheet is distinct from the cell membrane surrounding an individual cell.

concepts.name: Glandular epithelium and inward folding
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Epithelial cells can acquire additional specialisation as gland cells that secrete substances at the epithelial surface. Sometimes a portion of the epithelial sheet folds inward and forms a multicellular gland; this is glandular epithelium. Outside explanation: Secretion means releasing a substance produced by a cell, while multicellular describes a structure made of multiple cells.

concepts.name: Reading epithelial forms: shape, layers and cilia
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Figure 6.9 compares four separate blocks: a thin squamous sheet of flattened tile-like cells, multilayered stratified squamous tissue with flattened surface cells, a single cuboidal layer of approximately cube-shaped cells, and tall columnar cells bearing cilia on their free surface. Each block lies above a contrasting supporting base, and their vertical arrangement is not a developmental sequence; the accompanying table compares six epithelial types under location, structure and function. Outside explanation: Read 'simple' as one layer and 'stratified' as multiple layers, then examine the exposed surface cells to interpret the shape term.

concepts.name: Simple squamous epithelium
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries, appearing in the diagram as a thin, tile-like sheet. The table locates it in blood-vessel lining, capillaries, lung air-sac lining and Bowman's capsule of the kidney, and gives transport by diffusion and situations requiring minimal protection as its functional associations. Outside explanation: A thin cellular barrier offers a short distance for diffusion, linking this structure to exchange rather than substantial protection against abrasion.

concepts.name: Simple cuboidal epithelium
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Simple cuboidal epithelium occurs in the tubular lining of kidneys and glandular ducts and performs absorption and secretion. The table describes a single layer of short cylindrical cells, sometimes with microvilli as in proximal convoluted tubules, whereas the diagram shows approximately cube-shaped cells. Outside explanation: Microvilli increase the cell's exposed surface area and are different from the cilia illustrated on columnar cells.

concepts.name: Simple columnar and ciliated columnar epithelium
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: The table describes simple columnar epithelium as a single layer of tall, slender cells, often ciliated, and places it in digestive-tract and upper-respiratory-tract linings. Its listed functions are protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction; the diagram shows cilia as a fringe on the free upper surface. Outside explanation: Coordinated ciliary beating can move material along a surface, whereas microvilli chiefly provide additional surface area.

concepts.name: Stratified squamous epithelium and renewal
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Stratified squamous epithelium lines the mouth and vagina and provides protection through several layers of cells. Cells are continuously sloughed off and regenerated: older cells are pushed upwards and become flat, while the lower layer is columnar and metabolically active. The diagram therefore identifies this tissue by flattened surface cells above multiple layers, not by assuming that the lower cells are also flat.

concepts.name: Stratified cuboidal epithelium
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Stratified cuboidal epithelium is listed in mammary glands, sweat gland and salivary glands, with protection of ducts of various glands as its function. Its upper layer is cuboid, while other layers may be cuboidal or of other types. Identify the layered arrangement and upper-cell shape together rather than assuming that each layer has the same shape.

concepts.name: Stratified columnar epithelium
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Stratified columnar epithelium is listed in the male urethra and lobar ducts of salivary glands, and its functions are protection and secretion. A layer of columnar cells lies upon squamous, columnar or cuboidal epithelial cells. Compare it with stratified cuboidal epithelium by the exposed layer's shape and by the precise locations in the table.

concepts.name: Three muscle types and the comparison framework
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Muscular tissue helps movement, and the supplied table distinguishes skeletal, cardiac and visceral, or smooth, muscle. It compares their location, function, appearance and control, so identification requires a combination of features rather than a single visual clue. Outside explanation: Voluntary control concerns movement under conscious control, whereas involuntary activity does not ordinarily require a conscious command.

concepts.name: Skeletal muscle
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Skeletal muscle is located at the skeleton and serves movement, heat and posture under voluntary control. Its parallel fibres are striated and multinucleated with eccentric nuclei; the drawing shows a long cylindrical, unbranched fibre with repeated transverse bands and several nuclei. Outside explanation: 'Eccentric' here means away from the centre, so nucleus position is an additional identifying feature.

concepts.name: Cardiac muscle
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Cardiac muscle is located in the heart, pumps blood continuously and is involuntary. The table describes striations and one central nucleus, while the illustration shows branching, connected striated fibres with nuclei inside them. Its combination of striations with involuntary control distinguishes it from both skeletal and smooth muscle.

concepts.name: Visceral or smooth muscle
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Visceral, or smooth, muscle is listed in the G.I. tract, uterus, eye and blood vessels, with functions including peristalsis, blood-pressure regulation, pupil-size control and erection of hairs. It is involuntary, lacks striations and has one central nucleus; the drawing shows a spindle-shaped cell with tapering ends and an expanded middle. Outside explanation: Peristalsis is a coordinated wave of muscular contraction that moves contents along a passage such as the digestive tract.

concepts.name: Connective-tissue examples and diagram organisation
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Connective tissue supports, links and cushions, and Figure 6.10 presents five separate examples: blood cells at the upper left, compact bone at the lower left, hyaline cartilage beside bone, areolar tissue at the upper right and adipose tissue at the lower right. These panels are examples within a tissue category, not stages in a sequence. Outside explanation: Extracellular matrix means material outside cells and provides a useful framework for comparing the very different appearances of connective tissues.

concepts.name: White blood corpuscles and their visual identification
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: The blood-cell panel groups neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, lymphocyte and monocyte as different white blood corpuscles, showing variations in nuclei and cytoplasm; cytoplasm is labelled around the nucleus, and the nucleus is the dark-stained region. Neutrophil has a lobed nucleus, eosinophil is the upper-middle cell, basophil is the granular upper-right cell, lymphocyte has a large dark nucleus at the lower left, and monocyte is the large lower-middle cell with an indented nucleus. The partly legible parenthetical text under Neutrophil is uncertain and should not be required as a verified label.

concepts.name: Platelets and the red blood corpuscle label
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Platelets are shown as small clustered fragments to the right of the lower white blood cells, whereas a red blood corpuscle is drawn separately below the compact-bone units. Keep their identities distinct from the named white blood corpuscles and from the bone structures near the red-cell label. Outside explanation: Platelets participate in blood clotting, and red blood cells carry oxygen; these functions clarify the labels but are not stated in these supplied diagram items.

concepts.name: Compact bone: Haversian canals and canaliculi
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Compact bone is drawn as circular units with concentric rings around central Haversian canals and fine channels extending through the surrounding bone. A Haversian canal contains blood vessels and nerve fibres, whereas a canaliculus contains a slender process of a bone cell, or osteocyte. Distinguish the central canal from the fine channel by both position and contents; the nearby red blood corpuscle is a separately identified blood cell.

concepts.name: Hyaline cartilage: chondrocytes and matrix
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: The hyaline-cartilage panel shows rounded cells, some grouped together, within a pale surrounding matrix. A chondrocyte is the cartilage cell embedded in that matrix, while the label 'Hyaline matrix' identifies the surrounding material rather than the cell. Compare these rounded embedded cells with the concentric organisation of the compact-bone panel.

concepts.name: Areolar tissue: fibres and associated cells
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Areolar tissue is illustrated as a loose fibre network containing several cell types, with fine branching reticular fibres and thicker collagen fibres. The labelled cells are an elongated fibroblast, an irregular macrophage among the fibres, a rounded granular mast cell, and a rounded plasma cell near the right edge. Separate fibre labels from cell labels during identification: the network and its resident cells are different structural components.

concepts.name: Adipose tissue and adipocyte organisation
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Adipose tissue is shown as a group of large pale, fat-containing cells with dark nuclei near their margins. The fat-droplet label identifies the large pale interior, the nucleus labels point to the dark peripheral structures, and 'Adipocyte' identifies a complete fat-storage cell. Outside explanation: A large stored fat droplet occupies much of the cell's interior, helping explain the nucleus's peripheral position.

concepts.name: Neural tissue and the parts of successive neurons
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: Neural tissue responds to stimuli, and the signalling diagram identifies each neuron's cell body, a nucleus within it, branching dendrites, a long axon and terminal axon tips. An incoming axon belongs to a previous neuron, while the lower-left neuron's axon extends rightwards and upwards towards the dendrites of the next neuron, whose cell body and nucleus are also labelled. Outside explanation: In this pathway, dendrites receive incoming information, the cell body contains the nucleus, and the axon carries the impulse towards its terminal branches; the nucleus is not a step in the impulse's route.

concepts.name: Impulse direction and communication across synapses
concepts.core_explanation: Book basis: The open-ended question asks, 'How do neurons transmit impulses (send message to other cells)?', and the diagram answers the visible route through successive neurons: an incoming axon contacts a receiving dendritic region at the lower-left synapse, and blue electrical-signal arrows run along that neuron's axon towards axon tips contacting the next neuron's dendrites at the upper synapse. Outside explanation: In a typical chemical synapse, arrival of an electrical impulse at an axon terminal leads to neurotransmitter release across a small gap; the transmitter acts on the receiving cell's membrane and can initiate a new electrical signal. Book basis: Blue arrows show signal direction, whereas black pointer lines identify parts; the supplied question has no options or printed answer.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cells, tissues, organs and body systems
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach a cell as a structural unit, a tissue as an organised group of cells, an organ as a structure containing tissues, and a body system as cooperating organs. This supplies the organisational scale needed for the four tissue categories and their locations.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach the cell membrane as the cell boundary, cytoplasm as the material within it outside the nucleus, and the nucleus as the genetic-control compartment. Learners must distinguish whole cells, internal parts, multiple nuclei and the neuron's signalling route.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Covering, lining, cavities and compartments
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach covering as lying over a surface, lining as covering an internal surface, and a cavity as an internal space. Explain a compartment as a separated body region so that epithelial barrier functions have a concrete meaning.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cell shapes, layers and tissue surfaces
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach flattened, cube-like, tall slender, cylindrical and spindle-shaped forms, and contrast one cell layer with several layers. Identify the free surface, the lower or basal region, and central versus peripheral positions before interpreting diagrams.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Extracellular material, intercellular space and fibres
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach extracellular as outside cells, intercellular as between cells, matrix as surrounding extracellular material, and fibres as thread-like extracellular components. Explain a cell process as an extension of a cell; this distinguishes epithelial cementing material, basement membrane, connective matrix and bone-cell processes.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Diffusion across a thin barrier
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach diffusion as net movement down a concentration gradient and explain that a shorter path can facilitate exchange. This makes the single thin squamous layer's association with diffusion understandable.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Absorption, secretion, glands and ducts
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach absorption as taking substances across a surface, secretion as release of a substance from a cell, a gland as a secretory structure, and a duct as a passage carrying glandular output. Explain multicellular as composed of multiple cells.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cilia, microvilli and mucus
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach cilia as hair-like surface projections whose coordinated beating can move material, microvilli as small projections increasing surface area, and mucus as a slippery secretion. These definitions prevent confusion between surface-area enhancement and directed surface transport.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Blood vessels, capillaries and lung air sacs
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach blood vessels as blood-carrying passages, capillaries as small exchange vessels, and lung air sacs as gas-exchange spaces. These are the concrete sites needed to learn the simple squamous row.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Kidney tubules, proximal convoluted tubules and Bowman's capsule
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach Bowman's capsule as the cup-like beginning of a kidney filtration unit and kidney tubules as passages involved in processing the filtrate, with the proximal convoluted tubule as an early coiled segment. Keep capsule lining and tubular lining distinct when learning the epithelial examples.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Digestive and respiratory passages, urethra and named glands
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Locate the digestive passage, upper respiratory passage, male urethra, mammary glands, sweat glands and salivary glands at a simple anatomical level. Explain that lobar ducts are ducts associated with gland lobes, so the table's location labels can be understood rather than memorised as unfamiliar words.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cell division, metabolism, shedding and abrasion
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach cell division as production of new cells, metabolism as cellular chemical activity, shedding as loss of surface cells, and abrasion as surface wear. These ideas explain renewal of the protective stratified squamous lining.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Muscle contraction, muscle fibres and striations
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach contraction as force generation that can produce shortening or tension, muscle fibre as the elongated muscle-cell unit in this context, and striations as visible transverse bands. This supplies the vocabulary for appearance and movement without requiring molecular contraction mechanisms.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Voluntary and involuntary control
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach voluntary control as conscious control of an action and involuntary activity as activity that does not ordinarily require a conscious command. Use these meanings before comparing the muscle rows.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Skeleton, heart circulation and smooth-muscle target structures
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Locate the skeleton and heart, explain that the heart pumps blood, identify the uterus and the pupil as the eye's opening, and define blood pressure as pressure exerted by blood within vessels. Define peristalsis as a coordinated travelling contraction so the muscle functions can be interpreted.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Blood components and their broad roles
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Distinguish white blood cells associated with defence, red blood cells associated with oxygen transport, and platelets associated with clotting at damaged vessels. Treat these as explanatory foundations, not as functions printed beside the supplied blood-cell labels.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Connective-tissue cell names and matrix vocabulary
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach osteocyte as a bone cell, chondrocyte as a cartilage cell, and adipocyte as a fat-storage cell. Introduce collagen and reticular fibres as extracellular network components and fibroblast, macrophage, mast cell and plasma cell as distinct cell names, avoiding the assumption that fibre labels name cells.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Phagocytosis, inflammation and antibodies as optional vocabulary support
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: If immune terms are used to explain the labelled cells, first teach phagocytosis as engulfment of material, inflammation as a response to injury or infection, and antibodies as proteins involved in specific defence; plasma cells are antibody-secreting cells derived from B lymphocytes. These are outside clarifications, not additional functions asserted by the supplied areolar or blood-cell diagrams.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Lipids, fat storage and nuclear position
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach fat as a lipid stored within cells and usable as an energy reserve. Explain that a large intracellular droplet can occupy much of the cell interior, preparing learners to interpret the adipocyte's marginal nucleus.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Stimulus and a nerve impulse
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach a stimulus as a detectable change and a nerve impulse as an electrical signal travelling along a neuron's membrane. Explain that ions are charged particles whose movement across membranes contributes to electrical signalling; detailed action-potential phases are unnecessary here.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Separate neurons, synaptic gaps and neurotransmitter receptors
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach that communicating neurons remain separate cells, that a synapse is a specialised communication junction, and that neurotransmitters are chemical messengers acting on receiving-membrane receptors. This makes the transition from an electrical signal along an axon to communication with another cell understandable.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Reading labels, arrows and separate diagram panels
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach pointer lines as identifiers and directional arrows as indicators of movement or sequence, while recognising that adjacent panels may simply compare examples. This prevents treating the epithelial blocks or connective-tissue panels as developmental stages.

exam_focus.why: Book-based target: Four-way tissue classification and function matching provide the framework for direct questions and odd-one-out items.
Book-based target: Tight packing, minimal intercellular spaces and an extracellular basement membrane are distinctive structural statements; distinguish basement membrane from cell membrane.
Book-based target: Secretory specialisation and inward folding into a multicellular gland connect epithelial structure with gland formation.
Book-based target: Recognising flattened, cuboidal, stratified and ciliated columnar forms supports diagram questions; the blocks are comparisons, not sequential stages.
Book-based target: Match simple squamous structure and diffusion with capillaries, vessel lining, lung air sacs and Bowman's capsule.
Book-based target: Kidney tubules, glandular ducts, absorption, secretion and proximal-convoluted-tubule microvilli form a high-value matching set.
Book-based target: Tall single-layer cells, cilia, mucus secretion and directed movement are useful for structure–function questions; retain the table's stated locations.
Book-based target: Mouth and vagina, protective layers, active lower cells and flattened shedding surface cells support location and statement-combination questions.
Book-based target: Gland-associated locations and protection of ducts distinguish stratified cuboidal from simple cuboidal tissue.
Book-based target: Male urethra and lobar salivary ducts are distinctive locations; columnar surface cells need not imply identical lower layers.
Book-based target: The three muscle types must be compared simultaneously across location, function, appearance and control.
Book-based target: Voluntary, striated, parallel fibres with multiple eccentric nuclei distinguish skeletal muscle; retain heat and posture alongside movement.
Book-based target: Cardiac muscle is the key exception to associating striations with voluntary control; branching and a central nucleus aid identification.
Book-based target: Smooth muscle combines involuntary control, absent striations and spindle-shaped cells; peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size and hair erection are matching targets.
Book-based target: Blood, bone, cartilage, areolar tissue and adipose tissue belong within the connective-tissue examples despite their different appearances.
Book-based target: Recognise the five named white blood corpuscles and visible nuclear distinctions; do not require the uncertain neutrophil parenthetical text.
Book-based target: Platelet fragments and the separately drawn red blood corpuscle should not be misclassified as one of the named white blood cells.
Book-based target: Haversian canal versus canaliculus is a precise structure–contents distinction: vessels and nerve fibres versus an osteocyte process.
Book-based target: Chondrocyte identifies a cartilage cell, while hyaline matrix identifies its extracellular surroundings.
Book-based target: Distinguish collagen and reticular fibres from fibroblast, macrophage, mast cell and plasma cell; this supports diagram labelling and odd-one-out questions.
Book-based target: Large fat droplets, marginal nuclei and the adipocyte label are the defining features shown for adipose tissue.
Book-based target: Identify dendrites, cell body, nucleus, axon and axon tips across successive neurons, without treating the nucleus as part of the signal route.

Book-based target: This directly answers the supplied question and tests direction along the axon and contacts at synapses; the additional neurotransmitter mechanism must remain labelled as outside explanation.

notes.about: This review evaluates the chapter map for '10. Tissues and Its Types' against the 66 extracted items from pages 3 and 7 and the BIE rulebook for UPSC / State PCS learners.
key_questions: Are all 66 teachable and structural items accounted for in the concepts?
Are book facts and outside explanations cleanly separated and accurate at the UPSC/State PCS textbook level?
Do the relations, prerequisites, cross-references, and teaching order provide a logical, complete pedagogical structure?

decisions.decision: Pass the chapter map with no blocking issues.
decisions.reason: Every single item from p003-i1 to p007-i53 is included in the concepts, book vs. outside basis is rigorously marked, uncertainties in the source (such as the illegible text under Neutrophil and the cuboidal shape wording difference) are transparently handled, and the teaching progression is thorough and logical.

problems.problem: Concept c03 (Glandular epithelium and inward folding, from p003-i11) is placed after c10 (at the end of the epithelial section), even though it appears in the text before the epithelial classification diagram and table (c04 to c10) and is mentioned in the cuboidal/columnar rows (glandular ducts, mucus secretion).
problems.fix: Consider moving c03 right after c02 (or right after c04) so students understand what a gland and glandular epithelium are before encountering 'glandular ducts', 'sweat gland', 'salivary glands', and 'mucus secretion' in the epithelial comparison table (c06, c07, c09, c10).

problems.problem: The first cross-reference entry has from_item_id 'p003-i12' resolving to 'p003-i12' (a self-reference for Fig. 6.9).
problems.fix: Either remove the self-referential entry or link p003-i12 to the corresponding table item p003-i17 where the same epithelial types are compared.

checklist.note: Every statement is clearly marked as 'Book basis' or 'Outside explanation', and all outside additions (e.g., chemical synaptic transmission, diffusion distance, microvilli vs. cilia roles) are standard and accurate.
The map is comprehensive, preserving every table detail, diagram feature, and label with appropriate conceptual depth for UPSC / State PCS aspirants.

The maker's notes clearly state the unit's scope, key pedagogical decisions with reasons, and source uncertainties (such as the partially legible text under Neutrophil and the table vs. diagram description of cuboidal cells).
Nothing is cut short, merged away, or left as 'etc.'; all 66 items are explicitly mapped and explained.
